opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the hardest questions in the field right now, and honestly I don't think anyone has a clean answer yet.

Part of the problem is that "world model" means very different things to different people. For some, it's a video generator that looks physically plausible. For others, it's an interactive simulator you can play in. And for people like me, it's more about an internal representation: a system that actually understands how the world works, that can predict, plan, and reason about consequences. Those lead to very different product stories.

If you treat it as video generation or interactive content, there's an obvious near-term product: entertainment, games, creative tools. That's real, and people will pay for it. But I worry that if we optimize too hard for that, we end up building very good pixel renderers rather than models that understand the world. Looking right and being right are not the same thing.

The more meaningful applications, to me, are in embodied intelligence: robotics, autonomous systems, anything that has to act in the physical world. There, a world model is less a product than infrastructure. It's the thing that lets an agent imagine "what happens if I do this" before it does it. But that market moves slower, and the value only becomes visible once the whole system works end to end.

So the challenge is a mismatch in timing. The research needs patience, and the business wants a product now. I don't think the answer is to force a killer app too early. It's better to be honest that this is foundational work, find a few domains where even an imperfect world model creates real value, like simulation for training robots, and let the capability mature. Language models went through something similar: for years they were research artifacts, and then suddenly the product became obvious. I suspect world models will follow a similar path, though the "ChatGPT moment" might look quite different from what people expect.

r001.rationale: It calls product discovery one of the hardest questions, but does not compare it with the data challenge.

r002.rationale: It does not state that AR glasses functioning as a true personal assistant require a world model.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize language-model-only AR glasses as ChatGPT with a screen and voice interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we haven't found it yet, and I don't think that's a failure of imagination so much as a sign of where the technology actually is.

When people say "world model," they often mean very different things. Some mean a video generator that looks physically plausible. Some mean an interactive simulator you can walk around in. Some mean the representation inside an agent that lets it plan. These are not the same product, and I think a lot of the confusion around "what's the product" comes from collapsing them together.

The obvious first instinct is entertainment: games, interactive video, something like a playable Sora. And I do think that will exist, but I'm a little skeptical it's the thing that justifies the whole research program. Games already have very good engines. A learned simulator that is slower, less controllable, and occasionally hallucinates physics is not clearly better for a game designer than Unreal. It's interesting as a demo. It's less obviously a product.

The second direction, and the one I personally find more compelling, is world models as infrastructure for agents and robotics. If you can learn a model of how the world evolves, you can use it for planning, for data generation, for evaluating a policy before you deploy it in the real world. Here the "product" is not something a consumer touches. It's a component. And that changes how you think about success. You don't need photorealism. You need the model to be right about the things that matter for the downstream task, and wrong in ways that don't hurt.

That brings me to what I think is the actual challenge, which is representation. A lot of current world models operate in pixel space, and I think that's partly an accident of history, because pixels are what we have data for and what we can look at. But pixels are a terrible interface for reasoning. Most of the bits in a video are irrelevant to any decision anyone would make. So one question I keep coming back to is: what is the right space to model the world in? If you get that wrong, you can scale all you want and still end up with something that's impressive to look at and not that useful.

There's also a chicken-and-egg problem with data. Language models got lucky because the internet is a huge corpus of humans using language to accomplish things. There is no equivalent corpus of humans interacting with the physical world with their actions logged. So any world model product has to also be a data flywheel, and that constrains what the first product can be. It probably has to be something people want to use even before the model is good, so that their usage teaches the model.

So if I had to summarize: I think the mistake is to look for the product by asking "what can this generate?" I'd rather ask "what decision does this let someone make better?" The moment a world model changes a decision, whether that's a robot deciding where to put its hand or an engineer deciding not to run an expensive real-world test, that's where the product is. And we're closer to that in narrow domains than people think, and further from it in the general case than the demos suggest.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that “world model” describes a capability, but it doesn’t yet describe a product. A user doesn’t come to you and say, “I need a world model.” They have something they want to do, and the question is whether understanding and predicting the world makes that task substantially easier.

For example, you could imagine using one for simulation: testing what might happen if a robot takes a particular action. But then generating something that looks plausible isn’t enough. The prediction has to be useful for making a decision. That’s a much harder requirement, and it gives you a more concrete way to measure progress.

So I would start with a narrow use case where you can close that loop: predict something, take an action, observe the outcome, and see whether the model helped. The tension is that we want a very general model, but the first successful product might be quite specific. Finding that application is part of the research, because it forces you to figure out which capabilities actually matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that “world model” describes a capability, but it doesn’t yet describe a product. You can build a model that generates a very compelling video, but then you have to ask: Who needs this, and what can they do with it that they couldn’t do before?

For me, the interesting distinction is between generating something that looks plausible and predicting something reliably enough to support a decision. If you want to use a world model for planning, the question is: If I take this action, what happens? And can I trust the differences between the possible outcomes? That’s a much higher bar than visual quality.

So I would start with a narrow setting where you can measure whether the model is useful. Can it help someone test an idea faster? Can it reduce the amount of real-world interaction needed to learn a task? You need that feedback loop. Otherwise, it’s very easy to keep improving the demo without knowing whether you’re getting closer to a product.

I’m optimistic about the capability. I’m less sure that the first successful product will be called a world model. It might just be a tool that solves a very specific problem, with a world model underneath.
